props.subtitle: Isolate core domain logic from external technologies, frameworks, databases, and UI drivers

what.definition: An architectural pattern originated by Alistair Cockburn that isolates application core logic using inbound and outbound Ports and Adapters.
what.summary: Hexagonal Architecture (also known as Ports & Adapters) decouples core business domain logic from external dependencies like HTTP controllers, databases, message brokers, and third-party APIs through explicit contracts called Ports, implemented by Adapters.
bullets: Driving (Primary) Ports & Adapters handle incoming user requests.
Driven (Secondary) Ports & Adapters handle outgoing persistence and external service calls.
Domain logic stays pure with zero framework dependencies.

why.summary: Traditional layered architectures tend to leak database entities and framework concerns into application code, making software hard to test, refactor, or migrate. Ports & Adapters allow developers to test business logic completely in memory without databases or HTTP servers.
why.impact: Enables fast in-memory unit testing and painless framework migrations.

terms.shortDefinition: An entry point contract (interface) exposed by the Application Core that defines what tasks the domain can perform for external actors.
terms.detailedDefinition: Driving Ports define the explicit use-case boundary of the core application. External actors like REST controllers or CLI handlers invoke these contracts to trigger business logic.
terms.whyItMatters: Decouples entry points from concrete web framework handlers.

dialogue.user: How do REST controllers interact with core logic?
dialogue.aiThoughts: Evaluating dependency direction; HTTP controllers should invoke inbound Port interfaces, not domain entities directly.
dialogue.aiQuestion: Does the Express controller call the PlaceOrderPort interface or directly instantiate ORM models?

terms.shortDefinition: An exit point contract (interface) declared by the Application Core defining requirements for external infrastructure.
terms.detailedDefinition: Driven Ports allow the Domain Core to express persistence and external service needs without depending on concrete ORM classes or HTTP clients.
terms.whyItMatters: Enables replacing databases or third-party APIs without modifying business logic.

dialogue.user: How does the domain save data without knowing about SQL?
dialogue.aiThoughts: Checking Dependency Inversion; domain defines OrderRepositoryPort interface, infrastructure implements it.
dialogue.aiQuestion: Which layer owns the OrderRepositoryPort interface definition?

terms.shortDefinition: An external component (HTTP REST controller, CLI command, gRPC handler) that converts requests into Driving Port calls.
terms.detailedDefinition: Driving Adapters sit outside the Hexagon. They parse external protocol payloads (JSON, CLI flags, protobufs) and translate them into domain command invocations.
terms.whyItMatters: Allows supporting multiple UI drivers (Web, Mobile, CLI, gRPC) against the exact same core logic.

dialogue.user: Can we add a gRPC endpoint without rewriting the business logic?
dialogue.aiThoughts: Verifying multi-driver capability; adding a gRPC Driving Adapter simply calls existing Driving Ports.
dialogue.aiQuestion: Would adding a gRPC adapter require editing any code inside the domain hexagon?

terms.shortDefinition: A concrete implementation of a Driven Port interface that communicates with external technology.
terms.detailedDefinition: Driven Adapters implement Secondary Port contracts using specific libraries like Prisma, TypeORM, Redis, or Stripe SDKs.
terms.whyItMatters: Isolates vendor-specific dependencies and database query details outside the core domain.

dialogue.user: How do we test domain logic without connecting to PostgreSQL?
dialogue.aiThoughts: Evaluating test doubles; swap PostgresDrivenAdapter with InMemoryOrderAdapter.
dialogue.aiQuestion: Can we run unit tests using an InMemoryDrivenAdapter in under 10 milliseconds?

terms.shortDefinition: High-level domain modules do not depend on low-level infrastructure details; both depend on abstractions (Ports).
terms.detailedDefinition: Dependency Inversion flips traditional dependency direction: infrastructure depends on domain contracts, ensuring the core remains pure and isolated.
terms.whyItMatters: Prevents framework creep and database entities from leaking into application logic.

dialogue.user: Why is Dependency Inversion critical for long-term maintainability?
dialogue.aiThoughts: Analyzing software longevity; domain logic outlives framework versions and database drivers.
dialogue.aiQuestion: What happens to your domain code when you upgrade or switch web frameworks?

categories.title: Primary (Driving) Adapters
categories.subtitle: Inbound Request Adapters
categories.description: Adapters that drive application execution by taking external user or system inputs and calling Driving Ports.
categories.details: Driving Adapters sit at the entry edge of the Hexagon. They convert transport-level payloads (JSON over HTTP, CLI arguments, gRPC messages) into domain commands or queries, then invoke the application's Driving Ports.
categories.analogy: Like a TV Remote Control or Game Controller sending user inputs to the internal console.
categories.primaryFocus: Translating external triggers into internal domain use case calls.
inScope: REST API Controllers (Express / NestJS / Spring MVC)

categories.title: Secondary (Driven) Adapters
categories.subtitle: Outbound Infrastructure Adapters
categories.description: Adapters that are driven by the Application Core to interact with external storage, APIs, and infrastructure.
categories.details: Driven Adapters implement Secondary Ports defined by the domain. They handle SQL/NoSQL persistence, third-party REST API integrations, and event publishing.
categories.analogy: Like a Power Adapter or Cable converting wall outlet electricity into what your device needs.
categories.primaryFocus: Fulfilling data persistence and external infrastructure contracts defined by the domain.

categories.title: Testing Mocks & In-Memory Adapters
categories.subtitle: In-Memory Test Doubles
categories.description: Lightweight in-memory adapter implementations designed for fast unit/integration testing.
categories.details: Test Adapters implement Driven Ports using in-memory HashMaps or mocks. They allow running 100% of domain use cases without booting databases, Docker containers, or network connections.
categories.analogy: Like a flight simulator providing realistic controls without burning jet fuel.
categories.primaryFocus: Enabling fast, deterministic, zero-dependency unit tests for business logic.

props.title: The Mechanics of Dependency Inversion
paragraphs: In traditional layered software architectures, high-level business logic directly imports low-level database drivers, web frameworks, or external SDKs. This creates tight coupling, where a database schema update or framework upgrade forces breaking changes throughout the entire codebase.
Hexagonal Architecture flips this dependency direction upside down using **Dependency Inversion**:
**The Hexagon Core**: The center of the application contains domain entities, aggregates, and use case logic. It has **zero dependencies** on external libraries, web frameworks, or databases.

**Ports (Interfaces)**: The Core defines TypeScript/Java interfaces at its boundary. Inbound interfaces (*Driving Ports*) define what use cases exist. Outbound interfaces (*Driven Ports*) define what infrastructure data services the core needs.
**Adapters (Implementations)**: Adapters sit outside the hexagon boundary. Driving Adapters invoke Driving Ports, while Driven Adapters implement Driven Ports.

By keeping the Core independent of technology choices, you gain extreme testability: unit tests can instantiate domain services with fast in-memory adapters without needing a running database or HTTP server.

challenges.prompt: Fill in the blank fields to complete the explanation of Hexagonal Architecture mechanics:
challenges.template: In Hexagonal Architecture, the core business logic resides inside the domain hexagon and depends only on {zone-1}. External HTTP requests enter the system through {zone-2}, which invoke {zone-3}. Outbound infrastructure services like databases implement {zone-4}, allowing unit tests to swap real databases with {zone-5}.
challenges.explanation:
Correct! Excellent Hexagonal Architecture synthesis.
The core domain depends only on Port interfaces. External HTTP requests enter via Driving Adapters which invoke Driving Ports. Outbound infrastructure implements Driven Ports, allowing tests to easily swap real infrastructure for In-Memory Adapters.

questions.question: What is the primary role of a Driving (Primary) Port in Hexagonal Architecture?

choices.text: It exposes SQL queries to external clients.
choices.explanation: SQL queries belong in database adapters, not in driving ports.

choices.text: It acts as an inbound contract interface declaring use cases the domain offers to external actors.
choices.explanation: Driving Ports are inbound interfaces owned by the Application Core that define how external drivers (HTTP Controllers, CLI) can invoke use cases.

choices.text: It connects the database directly to the HTTP controller.
choices.explanation: Hexagonal Architecture strictly prohibits connecting HTTP controllers directly to databases.

choices.text: It parses HTML templates for web pages.
choices.explanation: HTML parsing is a UI presentation concern, completely outside driving port contracts.

questions.hint: Think about who initiates execution (inbound vs outbound).

questions.question: Why does Hexagonal Architecture invert dependencies for database access using Driven Ports?

choices.text: So the database schema determines the domain model.
choices.explanation: Database schema driving domain models is a anti-pattern that Hexagonal Architecture prevents.

choices.text: To allow the Domain Core to define its data requirements without depending on concrete ORMs or database drivers.
choices.explanation: Driven Ports allow the domain logic to specify repository contracts while concrete database adapters implement those contracts outside the hexagon.
Dependency inversion makes unit testing significantly easier and faster.

choices.text: To force all database queries to be written in GraphQL.
choices.explanation: GraphQL is a web API query layer, unrelated to persistence ports.

questions.hint: Consider how domain tests run without booting real SQL databases.

questions.question: Which component in Hexagonal Architecture is responsible for converting HTTP REST payloads into domain commands?

choices.explanation: Driven Adapters handle outbound infrastructure like databases or external web APIs.
Driven Ports are outbound interface definitions, not request handlers.
Driving Adapters (such as Express or Spring HTTP controllers) receive external HTTP requests and adapt them to call Driving Port use cases.
Domain Aggregates enforce business rules and consistency, unaware of HTTP protocols.

questions.hint: Who converts inbound HTTP requests before calling the port?
